title: Level 3 – Cyber Defender (Year 9)
_about: Written by Anish Shrestha (2) and Kiri Rāwiri (simulated). Draft for Cultural Guide review. Categories: SOC, DEV, WEB, ETH.

questions.text: What is social engineering?

options.D: Tricking people into giving information or access

questions.feedback: Social engineering targets people, not computers – by building trust and then exploiting it.

questions.scenario_text: A caller says they are from the school IT team. They say your account is broken and ask you to read out the 6-digit code just sent to your phone.
questions.text: What should you do?

options.B: Hang up and contact the school office using a number you already know
options.D: Post the code in a group chat

questions.feedback: Real IT staff never ask for your one-time codes. Verify using a contact you already know.

questions.scenario_text: A message from a new account says: "Kia ora cuz, it's me, your whanaunga (cousin)! My phone broke. Can you send me your school login so I can check something?"
questions.text: What is the best response?

options.A: Send the login – family helps family
options.D: Call or ask your cousin using their usual number or in person before doing anything

questions.feedback: Attackers pretend to be family to build trust. Verify first – and never share a login, even with family.

questions.text: Someone follows a staff member through a locked door without using their own card. What is this called?
questions.feedback: Tailgating is a physical social engineering trick. Don't hold secure doors open for people you don't know.

questions.text: Which are good countermeasures against social engineering? Choose ALL that apply.

options.A: Verify requests using a contact you already know
options.C: Act quickly when someone says it is urgent

questions.feedback: Verify, protect secrets and report. Urgency is a pressure trick – slow down instead.

questions.scenario_text: At a shopping mall you see a free USB charging port and a cable already plugged in.
questions.text: What is the safest choice?

options.A: Plug in your phone with the cable provided
options.B: Unlock your phone first so it charges faster
options.C: Use your own charger in a power socket, or a charge-only cable
options.D: Share your PIN with the shop

questions.feedback: Data can travel through USB. A tampered port could try to steal data ("juice jacking").

questions.text: What is the main risk of logging in to your email on free public Wi-Fi?

options.B: Others on the network may try to watch or intercept your traffic

questions.feedback: Avoid important logins on open Wi-Fi. Use mobile data or a trusted network.

questions.text: A new torch (flashlight) app asks for access to your contacts and microphone. What should you do?

options.A: Deny the permissions it does not need, or choose a different app

questions.feedback: Only give apps the permissions they really need.

questions.text: True or false: smart devices like home cameras should keep their factory default password.
questions.feedback: Default passwords are often public. Attackers have taken over thousands of IoT devices this way (for example the Mirai botnet).

questions.text: Which habits improve the physical security of your devices? Choose ALL that apply.

options.A: Lock your screen with a PIN or fingerprint
options.B: Leave your laptop unlocked in the library

questions.feedback: Locking, tracking and watching your devices keeps them and your data safe.

questions.text: A page shows "Click to win!" but an invisible button underneath changes your account settings. What is this trick?
questions.feedback: Clickjacking hides a real button under a fake one so you click it without knowing.

questions.scenario_text: A free-download website shows four big green "DOWNLOAD" buttons and many flashing ads.
questions.text: What is the safest way to get the app?

options.B: Click every button until one works
options.C: Download it from the official app store or the developer's real website

questions.feedback: Fake download buttons often lead to malware. Use official sources.

questions.text: A website you have never used asks "Allow notifications?" What is the safest answer?
questions.feedback: Notification spam is used to show fake virus warnings and scams. Block unknown sites.

questions.text: True or false: malicious adverts (malvertising) can appear even on websites you normally trust.
questions.feedback: Ads come from ad networks, so a bad ad can appear on a good website. Be careful what you click.

questions.text: Which actions help protect you from web tricks? Choose ALL that apply.

options.B: Download apps only from official stores
options.C: Click pop-ups that say you won something

questions.feedback: Updates, official stores and blocking notifications all reduce risk.

questions.text: What is intellectual property?

options.C: Work created by someone's mind, such as music, art, writing and software

questions.feedback: Intellectual property belongs to its creator and is protected by laws like copyright.

questions.scenario_text: A website offers a free "cracked" copy of a popular game that normally costs $79.
questions.text: Which statement is true?

options.A: It is illegal under the Copyright Act 1994 and cracked games often contain malware
options.B: It is fine because it is free
options.C: It is legal if you only play at home
options.D: It is legal if you delete it after a week

questions.feedback: Pirated software breaks copyright law and is a common way to spread malware.

questions.text: True or false: being anonymous online means your actions have no consequences.
questions.feedback: Anonymous accounts can often be traced, and harm to others is still real.

questions.text: You find a picture with a Creative Commons licence that says "Attribution required". What must you do to use it?
questions.feedback: Creative Commons lets you use work if you follow its rules – here, by giving credit.

questions.scenario_text: A student finds a way to get around the school internet filter and shares it with friends.
questions.text: Which statement best describes this?

options.B: It breaks the school's acceptable use policy and could expose others to harmful content

questions.feedback: School computers have rules to keep everyone safe. Report problems instead of bypassing controls.
